To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
progeny of sired selected on an economic beef carcass index had heavier carcasses with greater muscularity and greater animal value than progeny of unselected sires.
selection using a beef carcass index has beneficial effects on live animal measurements, meat proportions, calculated carcass values and animal values in male progeny.

selection of sires for an economic index based on carcass weight, feed intake and conformation and fat score had positive associations with carcass meat and value, as well as muscularity and fat depth in steer progeny.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of sire selection using an economic breeding index for beef production on live animal and carcass traits in progeny.
identifying the effects of sire genetic merit on the performance of progeny in a beef production system.

the effects of genetic improvement on economically important traits and their predictors, and the results of this study provide information to assist beef farmers in making informed breeding decisions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

progeny of high B CI sires have greater carcass meat proportion (P <0.05), calculated carcass value and animal value (P < 0001), greater muscularity scores after-weaning (P < 005), greater skeletal score and scanned muscle depth (P < 05) and greater plasma insulin concentrations (P < 01) than progeny from low BCI sired progeny.
the BCI is a useful tool in the genetic improvement of beef production.
selection for the BCI had a positive effect on the economically important traits in this study.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

progeny of sired by bulls with higher genetic merit for the beef carcass index had a more desirable carcass composition and higher calculated animal value, but there was no difference in the carcass composition or calculated animal value of progeny of bulls with higher genetic merits for carcass weight.
the progeny of high BCG sires were superior in terms of carcass quality and animal value, but the progeny of low BC sires had greater carcass fat proportions.
the progeny of the BCI selected sires were heavier, had greater muscle depth, more muscle tissue, less fat tissue and higher animal value than progeny from the low BCI selected sired group.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selection for the BCI in beef cattle is associated with positive changes in carcass composition and value, and that these changes are more evident in steer progeny.
the use of the BCI in Ireland has resulted in the production of progeny with carcasses of greater value, which is a desirable outcome of a selection programme for beef cattle in Ireland.

selection for BCI in beef production systems is beneficial for improving the carcass value of progeny, but the effect of selection for BCI on progeny performance is not the same across production systems.
